# Convert complete or legacy manuscript labels back to the stable internal
# codes used by the Results-section filters. This makes the QMD compatible
# with CSV outputs produced before or after the labels were expanded.
morph_code <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)

  x |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:8th|8|eight|eighth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "eighth"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:9th|9|nine|ninth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "ninth"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:10th|10|ten|tenth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "tenth"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex("\\bfemale(?:s)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE),
      "female"
    )
}

# Convert internal or legacy morph codes to complete manuscript labels.
# This function accepts labels from old and new CSV outputs.
morph_label <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)

  x |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:8th|8|eight|eighth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "Eighth instar"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:9th|9|nine|ninth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "Ninth instar"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex(
        "\\b(?:10th|10|ten|tenth)(?:[-\\s]+instar)?\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      ),
      "Tenth instar"
    ) |>
    stringr::str_replace_all(
      stringr::regex("\\bfemale(?:s)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE),
      "Female"
    )
}

# Expand morph labels only in label columns, never in formatted statistics.
# Applying this to all strings would turn 88.8% into 88.Eighth instar%.
normalize_table_labels <- function(x) {
  x <- as.data.frame(x)
  label_columns <- grepl("^(group|contrast|pair)$|morph", names(x),
                         ignore.case = TRUE)
  x[label_columns] <- lapply(
    x[label_columns],
    function(column) {
      if (is.character(column) || is.factor(column)) {
        morph_label(column)
      } else {
        column
      }
    }
  )

  x
}

read_result <- function(filename) {
  readr::read_csv(
    file.path(tables_dir, filename),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      dplyr::across(
        where(is.character),
        morph_code
      )
    )
}

fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
}

fmt_p <- function(p, digits = 3) {
  if (is.na(p)) return("p = NA")
  if (p < 0.001) return("p < 0.001")
  paste0("p = ", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = digits))
}


# Format manuscript tables for Word with no vertical rules, a rule at the
# top of the table, a rule beneath the column headings, and a closing rule.
manuscript_table <- function(x, align = NULL) {
  x <- normalize_table_labels(x)

  rule <- officer::fp_border(color = "black", width = 0.75)

  ft <- flextable::flextable(x) |>
    flextable::font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") |>
    flextable::fontsize(size = 10, part = "all") |>
    flextable::border_remove() |>
    flextable::bold(part = "header") |>
    flextable::hline_top(border = rule, part = "header") |>
    flextable::hline_bottom(border = rule, part = "header") |>
    flextable::hline_bottom(border = rule, part = "body") |>
    flextable::padding(padding = 2, part = "all") |>
    flextable::autofit() |>
    flextable::set_table_properties(
      layout = "autofit", width = 1,
      opts_word = list(split = FALSE, repeat_headers = TRUE)
    )

  if (!is.null(align)) {
    if (length(align) != ncol(x)) {
      stop("The alignment vector must have one entry per table column.", call. = FALSE)
    }

    # flextable::align() requires full alignment names. Accept common
    # one-letter abbreviations as a convenience, but translate them first.
    align_key <- c(
      l = "left", left = "left",
      c = "center", centre = "center", center = "center",
      r = "right", right = "right",
      j = "justify", justify = "justify"
    )
    align <- unname(align_key[tolower(align)])

    if (anyNA(align)) {
      stop(
        "Table alignment must be one of: left, center, right, or justify.",
        call. = FALSE
      )
    }

    for (j in seq_along(align)) {
      ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = j, align = align[[j]], part = "all")
    }
  }

  ft
}

# Format an F-test from the joint leg ANOVA (columns already renamed in setup).
fmt_f <- function(row, digits = 2) {
  paste0(
    "$F_{", fmt_num(row$num_df, 0), ",", fmt_num(row$den_df, 2), "} = ",
    fmt_num(row$f_value, digits), ", ", fmt_p(row$p_value), "$"
  )
}

# Format an F-test from either nested-model comparison table schema.
fmt_f_nested <- function(row, digits = 2) {
  residual_df <- if ("full_residual_df" %in% names(row)) {
    row$full_residual_df
  } else {
    row$residual_df
  }
  paste0(
    "$F_{", fmt_num(row$numerator_df, 0), ",",
    fmt_num(residual_df, 0), "} = ",
    fmt_num(row$F, digits), ", ", fmt_p(row$p_value), "$"
  )
}

# Format an F-test from a Type III ANOVA table
# (columns: NumDF, DenDF, `F value`, `Pr(>F)`).
fmt_f_anova <- function(row, digits = 2) {
  paste0(
    "$F_{", fmt_num(row$NumDF, 0), ",",
    fmt_num(row$DenDF, 1), "} = ",
    fmt_num(row$`F value`, digits), ", ", fmt_p(row$`Pr(>F)`), "$"
  )
}

get_term <- function(tab, term_name) {
  out <- tab |> filter(.data$term == term_name)
  if (nrow(out) != 1) stop("Could not uniquely locate model term: ", term_name, call. = FALSE)
  out
}

get_vs_female <- function(tab, group_name, leg_name = NULL) {
  out <- tab |>
    filter(
      stringr::str_detect(
        .data$contrast,
        stringr::regex(
          paste0("^", group_name, "\\s*-\\s*female$"),
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      )
    )
  if (!is.null(leg_name)) out <- out |> filter(.data$leg == leg_name)
  if (nrow(out) != 1) {
    stop(
      "Could not uniquely locate contrast for ", group_name,
      if (!is.null(leg_name)) paste0(" within ", leg_name) else "",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
  out
}

effect_text <- function(row, positive = "longer", negative = "shorter") {
  pct <- row$percent_difference
  direction <- ifelse(pct >= 0, positive, negative)
  paste0(
    fmt_num(abs(pct), 1), "% ", direction,
    " (Holm-adjusted ", fmt_p(row$p.value), ")"
  )
}

group_labels <- c(
  eighth = "Eighth-instar males",
  ninth  = "Ninth-instar males",
  tenth  = "Tenth-instar males"
)

describe_vs_female <- function(
    tab,
    percent_column = "percent_difference",
    positive = "larger",
    negative = "smaller"
) {
  tab <- tab |>
    filter(stringr::str_detect(.data$contrast, "female")) |>
    mutate(
      group_key   = str_trim(str_remove(.data$contrast, "\\s*-\\s*female$")),
      group_label = unname(group_labels[.data$group_key]),
      pct         = .data[[percent_column]],
      direction   = if_else(.data$pct >= 0, positive, negative),
      clause      = paste0(
        .data$group_label, " were ", fmt_num(abs(.data$pct), 1), "% ",
        .data$direction, " than females (Holm-adjusted ",
        map_chr(.data$p.value, fmt_p), ")"
      )
    )
  paste(tab$clause, collapse = "; ")
}

# ── Allometric slope display ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
trend_column <- names(joint_slopes)[str_detect(names(joint_slopes), "\\.trend$")][1]

# ── Segment-level summary ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
segment_tests_display <- segment_tests |>
  mutate(
    Segment = str_remove(.data$analysis, ":.*$"),
    Result  = if_else(
      .data$p_value < alpha, "Different slopes", "Common slope adequate"
    )
  ) |>
  select(Segment, numerator_df, full_residual_df, F, p_value, Result)

significant_segments <- segment_tests_display |>
  filter(.data$p_value < alpha) |>
  pull(.data$Segment) |>
  stringr::str_to_lower()

segment_result_text <- if (length(significant_segments) == 0) {
  "None of the six segment-level analyses supported group-specific allometric slopes."
} else {
  segment_list <- if (length(significant_segments) == 1) {
    significant_segments
  } else if (length(significant_segments) == 2) {
    paste(significant_segments, collapse = " and ")
  } else {
    paste0(
      paste(head(significant_segments, -1), collapse = ", "),
      ", and ", tail(significant_segments, 1)
    )
  }
  paste0(
    "Group-specific allometric slopes were supported for ",
    segment_list,
    "; the remaining segment models were adequately described by common slopes."
  )
}

  filter(.data$analysis_tier == "primary") |>

  integration_matrix_omnibus$matrix_type == "covariance"][1]

}
six_cov_matrix_p <- integration_matrix_six$p_value[

dominant_trait_names <- c(

  filter(.data$component == "PC1") |>
  mutate(

# Abstract

Alternative mating strategies may involve coordinated divergence in locomotor and sensory morphology as well as weaponry. I examined these relationships in Wellington tree wētā (*Hemideina crassidens*), whose male morphs mature at the eighth, ninth or tenth instar and differ in weapon size and mating behaviour. Using field-collected adults, I compared body-size-adjusted leg lengths, eye length and tympanic organ area among females and the three male morphs. Leg and sensory dimensions generally increased from eighth- to tenth-instar males, contrary to the prediction that small searching males would have the largest supporting structures. Tenth-instar males also showed greater anterior leg allocation than females. A dominant axis captured `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_proportion, 1)`% of adjusted group-effect variation, although smaller departures from that axis were detectable. All `r sign_total` within-group correlations among the five non-head traits were positive. No covariance- or correlation-matrix difference was detected in this primary trait set, but adding head size revealed a covariance-magnitude difference. Head size was positively associated with leg length, whereas male weapon–ear associations remained imprecise. Comparisons with females at the same terminal instar distinguished a within-male instar gradient from a sex-associated difference, without isolating a causal weapon effect. These results describe predominantly coordinated phenotypic divergence. They do not establish uniform covariance structure across all traits or exclude allocation costs masked by variation in resource acquisition.

**Keywords:** alternative mating strategies; allometry; morphological integration; phenotypic covariance; sexual selection; trait compensation; wētā

# Introduction

Alternative mating strategies allow males to achieve reproductive success through different routes to mate competition. Large or well-armed males may defend females or reproductive resources, whereas smaller males obtain matings through sneaking, satellite behaviour or active searching [@gross1996; @shuster2003; @oliveira2008]. These strategies can involve coordinated differences in morphology, physiology, behaviour and life history, rather than variation in weaponry alone [@west-eberhard2003]. Understanding this coordination requires distinguishing differences among morph means from covariance among individuals within each morph.

Exaggerated sexual structures can impose developmental or performance costs. Secondary sexual trait compensation occurs when enlargement of supporting structures mitigates those costs [@tomkins2005; @husak2011]. Alternatively, structures competing for limited developmental resources may trade off [@nijhout1998; @emlen2001a; @moczek2004], while variation in resource acquisition can elevate several costly traits together [@bonduriansky2003; @vannoordwijk1986]. Positive phenotypic covariance therefore need not demonstrate adaptive compensation, and its presence does not exclude an allocation trade-off. Developmental switches may also alter trait covariance among morphs, creating different patterns of integration within the same body plan [@snell-rood2010; @rohner2020].

Studies of weapon-bearing insects illustrate this variation. Horn length covaries positively with leg morphology in dung beetles, sometimes more strongly in major than minor males [@tomkins2005; @rohner2020]. Relatively long-horned rhinoceros beetles also have relatively long wings and foretibiae, but horn size is unrelated to eye size after body-size adjustment [@mccullough2013]. In the stag beetle *Prosopocoilus inclinatus*, weapon size is integrated with eye size in major males and with foreleg length in minor males [@ito2017]. Thus, weapon enlargement need not be accompanied by the same supporting traits in every morph.

Locomotor and sensory demands may differ between males that search for mates and those that defend them. Searching males could benefit from structures that facilitate movement and detection, whereas defenders could benefit from appendages that provide support during combat. In the desert bee *Centris pallida*, small males rely primarily on vision for mate detection and have relatively larger eyes than large males, which rely more on chemosensory cues [@barrett2021; @barrett2026]. Defending males might nevertheless require substantial sensory investment for assessing rivals or mating sites. Examining locomotor and sensory traits together can reveal whether strategy-associated divergence is broadly coordinated or differs among functional systems.

The Wellington tree wētā, *Hemideina crassidens*, is a flightless, nocturnal orthopteran in which females shelter communally in tree cavities, hereafter galleries. Males use enlarged heads and mandibles in contests for female-occupied galleries; larger weapons generally confer an advantage in escalated fights [@kelly2005a; @kelly2006d; @kelly2010]. Males express three genetically polymorphic, irreversible morphotypes through maturation at the eighth, ninth or tenth juvenile instar [@nason2020; @kelly2024]. Tenth-instar males have the most exaggerated weapons and commonly defend galleries. Eighth-instar males may circumvent defenders or search vegetation for undefended females; ninth-instar males combine fighting and sneaking according to social context [@wilson2019; @kelly2025]. Similar average reproductive fitness among strategies is consistent with maintenance of the polymorphism [@nason2020].

I compared the relative expression and allometry of fore-, mid- and hindleg lengths, eye length and tympanic organ area among these male morphs and females. Females provide a reference sharing the general body plan without the exaggerated male weapons. I tested whether groups differed in anterior–posterior leg allocation and whether composite head size, used as a proxy for weapon investment, covaried with leg or sensory size after body-size adjustment. These are phenotypic comparisons, not direct measurements of resource allocation or performance.

Three hypotheses guided the comparisons. Under a searching-and-detection hypothesis, eighth-instar males should possess relatively longer legs and larger sensory structures, with weapon investment weakly or negatively associated with these traits. Under a positive-integration hypothesis, tenth-instar males should express larger weapons and supporting structures, with positive within-group weapon–trait associations that may be strongest in the most heavily armed morph. Under a shared-growth-axis hypothesis, divergence should be concentrated in one dominant dimension, with predominantly positive within-group covariance and limited restructuring among groups. The latter two hypotheses can produce similar phenotypic patterns and cannot be separated solely by positive covariance.

Male morphs differ in both weapon size and terminal instar number, so comparisons among males cannot separate those attributes. Females mature at the tenth instar, allowing a comparison with tenth-instar males at matched instar number. I therefore estimated a within-male per-instar gradient and a tenth-instar male–female contrast in the same model. This distinguishes two descriptive components of divergence, but the matched contrast differs in sex as well as weapon expression and cannot isolate a causal weapon effect. I also examined the dimensionality of adjusted group differences and within-group covariance, and assessed whether ninth-instar males were intermediate between the other male morphs.

# Materials and methods

## Study site and specimen collection

The sample comprised 313 adult *H. crassidens* collected haphazardly at night from vegetation on Te Pākeka/Maud Island, New Zealand (41°02′ S, 173°54′ E), during March and April 2016. The island is a 309-ha scientific reserve in the Marlborough Sounds, free of introduced mammalian predators. Vegetation sampling may under-represent gallery occupants, and the analysed male morph composition differed from published reference samples. Collection microhabitat and search effort were not retained in sufficient detail to correct this potential selection bias. The results therefore describe the sampled adults; fixed adult morphology does not guarantee that either group means or within-group covariance is representative of the population.

Adult males were assigned to eighth-, ninth- or tenth-instar morphotypes using mixture models of head length fitted with *mixsmsn* [@prates2013], following @kelly2010 and @kelly2026. Individuals were euthanized by freezing at −20 °C. The head, pronotum and both legs of each pair were dissected and stored together in a labelled tube preserving the individual's identifier.

Institutional animal-ethics approval was not required for this invertebrate study. The Department of Conservation provided permits for specimen collection and access to Te Pākeka/Maud Island.

## Imaging and morphological measurements

Each dissected structure was photographed with a Canon EOS 5D Mark IV camera, Canon EF 100 mm f/2.8L IS USM Macro lens and Canon MT-26EX-RT flashes. The camera was mounted approximately 40 cm above the specimen with its sensor parallel to the imaging surface. A ruler and specimen identifier were photographed in the same plane; images were calibrated from the ruler and given a 5-mm scale bar using ImageJ.

Measurements were made in Fiji [@schindelin2012]. Linear measurements used consistent anatomical landmarks and the straight-line tool; tympanic organ area was obtained by tracing the membrane perimeter (@fig-morphological-measurements). Traits were pronotum length, head length and width, eye length, and femur and tibia lengths for all three leg pairs. Bilateral structures were measured separately and averaged; the available side was used when only one side was measured. Total leg length was the sum of the corresponding femur and tibia lengths.

## Measurement repeatability

Forty-eight individuals were remeasured twice from the original images, giving three measurements per trait. The sample contained 12 individuals from each sex or morph group, one from each of 12 recorded size strata. Image order was randomized independently for each round, and previous measurements were not consulted.

For each trait, a random-intercept model estimated repeatability as $R=V_{\mathrm{individual}}/(V_{\mathrm{individual}}+V_{\mathrm{residual}})$. Morph-adjusted and measurement-round-adjusted models, absolute-agreement coefficients, measurement error, round-pair bias and order diagnostics are reported in the supplement (Table S1).

## Statistical analysis

Analyses used R [@rcoreteam2025], with *tidyverse* for preparation and visualization [@wickham2019], base R for ordinary least-squares models, *nlme* for generalized least squares [@R-nlme], and *emmeans* for adjusted means, trends and contrasts [@lenth2019package]. Diagnostics used *performance*, *see* and *broom* [@ludecke2021; @ludecke2021a; @robinson2014]. Females and the three male morphs formed the four levels of `group`.

Pronotum length represented structural body size. Composite head size was the geometric mean of head length and width. Tympanic organ area was square-root transformed to a linear dimension, and all continuous morphological variables were then natural-log transformed. Log–log slopes are consequently allometric exponents. Log pronotum length was centred at 7.2 mm, $\log P_c=\log(\mathrm{pronotum})-\log(7.2)$, within the body-size range shared by all groups. Adjusted means at $\log P_c=0$ thus represent interpolation. Data were checked for duplicate identifiers, unexpected labels, missing or nonpositive measurements and implausible ranges; missing observations were excluded per model.

### Dimensionality and covariance

The primary multivariate trait set comprised foreleg, midleg and hindleg length, linearised tympanic organ size and eye length. Head size was excluded because head length contributes to morph assignment. These analyses used the `r n_integration` individuals complete for all five traits. The dimensionality and matrix tests are exploratory descriptions of integration, distinct from the planned marginal contrasts below.

A multivariate model with group-specific body-size slopes estimated adjusted group differences at 7.2 mm. Traits were standardized by pooled residual standard deviations, and the three male groups were expressed as contrasts with a shared female reference. A design-weighted singular value decomposition quantified the fraction of group-effect variation captured by a rank-one approximation. A test based on `r rank_one_n_perm` randomizations permuted multivariate residual vectors around the fitted rank-one model and assessed departures from rank one. This procedure preserves the shared female reference and does not treat repeated copies of females as independent groups. Sensitivity analyses added head size and repeated the six-trait analysis on unstandardized log measurements (Table S7).

Principal component analysis described individual-level size-adjusted variation. For each trait, the adjusted value was its group-specific fitted value at 7.2 mm plus its residual, retaining adjusted group differences while removing the estimated within-group body-size slope. Parallel analysis compared observed correlation-matrix eigenvalues with the 95th percentiles obtained by independently permuting trait columns in `r pca_permutations` randomizations. This individual-level ordination and the rank-one analysis of group effects address different sources of variation.

Within-group covariance and correlation matrices were calculated from residuals of group-specific trait–body-size regressions. Omnibus and pairwise Frobenius-distance tests used `r matrix_permutations` randomizations of residual-vector group membership, retaining observed group sizes. Pairwise p-values were adjusted by Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg procedures. Adding head size tested sensitivity to trait selection; matrix similarities and rarefaction assessed descriptive structure and unequal sample sizes (Tables S8–S9). I also counted positive and negative within-group pairwise correlations and summarized their range and mean. This sign audit is descriptive: positive phenotypic covariance can mask allocation costs when resource acquisition varies among individuals [@vannoordwijk1986].

### Leg allometry and allocation

Separate leg models compared common and group-specific slopes using nested-model $F$-tests. The principal analysis of relative leg allocation was a repeated-trait generalized least-squares model,

$$
\log(\mathrm{leg\ length})\sim\log P_c\times\mathrm{group}\times\mathrm{leg}.
$$

Each individual contributed up to three leg measurements. An unstructured residual covariance matrix allowed separate residual variances for the three leg pairs and freely estimated within-individual correlations. It fitted better than heterogeneous compound symmetry (Table S10). Models used restricted maximum likelihood, with type III joint tests and approximate Satterthwaite denominator degrees of freedom. The three-way interaction tested whether group differences in body-size slope depended on leg identity.

Adjusted means were estimated by leg pair at 7.2 mm and exponentiated to geometric means. Exponentiated contrasts are ratios, with values above one indicating a larger estimate for the first-named group. Planned comparisons contrasted eighth- with tenth-instar males, ninth-instar males with the eighth/tenth midpoint, and tenth-instar males with females. Difference-in-differences contrasts compared foreleg with hindleg, midleg with hindleg, and the mean of the anterior leg pairs with hindleg. These quantify relative anterior–posterior allocation rather than absolute leg size. Separate femur and tibia models and detailed slope comparisons were exploratory (Tables S14–S16).

### Weapon and sensory associations

Weapon–leg integration was tested by adding raw log composite head size to the repeated-trait model,

$$
\log L\sim(\log P_c+\log H)\times G\times J,
$$

where $L$ is leg length, $H$ is composite head size, $G$ is group and $J$ is leg identity.

The same unstructured residual covariance was retained. Group- and leg-specific partial head-size slopes controlled for pronotum length and were compared within the relevant contrast families. Positive slopes describe positive phenotypic integration; negative slopes would be consistent with a morphological trade-off. Neither sign alone identifies a developmental mechanism. Earlier residual-predictor models are retained as exploratory checks, not as the basis of the principal weapon–leg inference.

Body-size-adjusted sensory models related log-linearised ear size and log eye length to $\log P_c$, group and their interaction. Common- and group-specific-slope models were compared by nested $F$-tests, and means were estimated at 7.2 mm. Eye estimates were exponentiated to lengths. Ear estimates were returned to area as $\exp(2\widehat{\mu})$, and ear contrast ratios were squared after exponentiation.

Local associations were tested in one-stage models containing group-specific body-size effects plus raw log foretibia length for the ear or raw log head size for the eye. Each anatomical predictor was allowed to interact with group, and a nested-model test compared this with a common partial slope. The corresponding ear model with head size tested weapon–ear covariance. These models distinguish size-adjusted associations from shared body size but cannot identify adaptive integration, resource allocation or developmental independence. Head size also reflects feeding structures and the substrate bearing the eyes, not weaponry alone.

### Instar-matched comparisons and precision

Each log trait was modelled as

$$
\log(\mathrm{trait})\sim\log P_c+\mathrm{instar}_c+\mathrm{sex},
$$

where $\mathrm{instar}_c$ is terminal instar number minus ten. The instar coefficient describes the within-male change per additional instar; the sex coefficient describes tenth-instar males relative to females at matched instar number. Their difference was tested directly. These are contrasts on a common log scale, not estimates of independently manipulated developmental and weapon effects. The latter is termed the instar-matched weapon component for continuity, but it includes any other sex-associated differences. One additional instar and the male–female comparison are also different biological contrasts, so their relative coefficients are not proportions of a causal variance partition.

The same decomposition was fitted jointly across leg pairs with the previously described residual covariance and fixed effects $(\log P_c+\mathrm{instar}_c+\mathrm{sex})\times\mathrm{leg}$. Estimated marginal means and trends are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Planned leg and allocation contrasts, weapon–leg slopes and male weapon–ear slopes are accompanied by approximate minimum detectable effects at 80% power and $\alpha=0.05$, calculated from observed standard errors and reference $t$ quantiles. These describe precision conditional on the fitted model; they do not turn a nonsignificant result into evidence of equivalence. Exploratory equivalence tests used specified illustrative regions (Tables S5 and S13).

### Inference and diagnostics

Holm adjustments were applied within the reported contrast families, including male–female, male-strategy and allocation contrasts, and across the five traits within each component of the instar-matched decomposition. The cross-analysis multiplicity audit is a separate sensitivity analysis (Table S12). Interpretation considered effect direction, confidence intervals and precision as well as $\alpha=0.05$; exploratory tests were not treated as additional confirmatory evidence.

Graphical diagnostics assessed residual normality, variance and residual–fitted relationships; variance-inflation diagnostics assessed collinearity. Cook's distance above $4/n$, leverage above $2p/n$, or an absolute standardized residual above 3 flagged observations for inspection, where $n$ is sample size and $p$ the number of coefficients. These criteria did not trigger automatic deletion.


# Results

## Sample composition and body-size overlap

The analysis included `r total_n` individuals across four groups (@tbl-group-summary). Pronotum lengths overlapped from `r fmt_num(common_body_size$common_lower, 2)` to `r fmt_num(common_body_size$common_upper, 2)` mm, encompassing the `r fmt_num(common_body_size$reference_pronotum, 1)`-mm reference used for adjusted comparisons.

## Dimensionality and covariance

For the five non-head traits, the dominant axis captured `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_proportion, 1)`% of design-weighted group-effect variation (@tbl-integration-structure). The remaining variation exceeded the rank-one randomization distribution (`r fmt_p(rank_one_p)`; `r rank_one_n_perm` randomizations), indicating smaller but detectable departures from a single axis. Across the `r rank_one_n_scenarios` trait-set and scaling scenarios, the rank-one share ranged from `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_share_min, 1)`% to `r fmt_num(100 * rank_one_share_max, 1)`% (Table S7).

Parallel analysis of individual-level adjusted measurements retained `r n_components_retained` component, explaining `r fmt_num(100 * pc1_variance, 1)`% of variance. The second eigenvalue (`r fmt_num(pc2_eigenvalue, 2)`) was below its randomization threshold (`r fmt_num(pc2_random, 2)`). All five first-component loadings had the same sign, describing coordinated variation in leg and sensory dimensions. This result concerns individual-level variation and does not negate the smaller departure from rank one detected among adjusted group means.

In the primary five-trait analysis, no difference was detected among groups in covariance matrices (`r fmt_p(cov_matrix_p)`) or correlation matrices (`r fmt_p(cor_matrix_p)`; `r matrix_permutations` randomizations), and no pairwise comparison survived Holm adjustment (Table S8). When head size was restored in the six-trait sensitivity analysis, a covariance-matrix difference was detected (`r fmt_p(six_cov_matrix_p)`), but a correlation-matrix difference was not (`r fmt_p(six_cor_matrix_p)`). The absence of a detected difference therefore applies to the primary non-head trait set, not to all measured morphology.

All `r sign_positive_total` of the `r sign_total` within-group pairwise correlations among the five adjusted traits were positive (@tbl-sign-audit). Mean correlations ranged from `r fmt_num(mean_cor_min, 2)` to `r fmt_num(mean_cor_max, 2)` among groups, with a minimum individual correlation of `r fmt_num(sign_min_cor, 2)`. This audit found no negative phenotypic covariance in the primary trait set. It neither establishes the absence of allocation costs nor demonstrates that covariance matrices are equivalent among groups.

## Locomotor morphology

### Relative allocation among leg pairs

Group differences depended strongly on leg identity in the repeated-trait model (`r fmt_f(leg_group_leg)`). Male–female differences therefore varied among forelegs, midlegs and hindlegs (@fig-adjusted-traits; Table S14). At the common body size, forelegs of eighth-, ninth- and tenth-instar males were respectively `r effect_text(fore_eighth)`, `r effect_text(fore_ninth)` and `r effect_text(fore_tenth)` than those of females. Corresponding midleg differences were `r effect_text(mid_eighth)`, `r effect_text(mid_ninth)` and `r effect_text(mid_tenth)`. Hindleg differences were `r effect_text(hind_eighth)`, `r effect_text(hind_ninth)` and `r effect_text(hind_tenth)`.

Tenth-instar males had longer legs than eighth-instar males across all three pairs. Eighth-instar forelegs were `r fmt_num(abs(strat_eighth_tenth_fore$percent_difference), 1)`% shorter (Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(strat_eighth_tenth_fore$p.value)`) and hindlegs `r fmt_num(abs(strat_eighth_tenth_hind$percent_difference), 1)`% shorter (`r fmt_p(strat_eighth_tenth_hind$p.value)`). Ninth-instar estimates were near the eighth/tenth midpoint. Exploratory two-one-sided tests supported equivalence within a ±2.5% region for all three pairs (largest `r fmt_p(leg_equiv_worst_p)`; Table S13). The largest absolute midpoint contrast was `r fmt_num(midpoint_obs_max, 1)`%, compared with a maximum minimum-detectable difference of `r fmt_num(midpoint_mde_max, 1)`% (@tbl-precision-leg). Equivalence here is specific to the chosen region, not evidence of identical means.

The planned anterior–posterior allocation contrasts among male morphs were not supported (all Holm-adjusted p-values at least `r sprintf("%.3f", alloc_within_male_min_p)`). Tenth-instar males nevertheless showed an anterior shift relative to females: their foreleg-to-hindleg ratio was `r fmt_num(alloc_tenth_female_fore_hind$percent_difference, 1)`% greater (ratio of ratios `r fmt_num(alloc_tenth_female_fore_hind$ratio_of_ratios, 2)`; Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(alloc_tenth_female_fore_hind$p.value)`). All three planned tenth-instar male–female allocation contrasts were supported (largest Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(max(alloc_tenth_female$p.value))`).

### Allometric variation

All estimated group-by-leg slopes were below one (@fig-leg-allometries; Table S15). The body-size-by-group interaction was supported (`r fmt_f(leg_size_group)`), but the body-size-by-group-by-leg interaction was not (`r fmt_f(leg_three_way)`). Thus, some group variation in scaling was detected without clear evidence that it differed by leg pair. Tenth-instar males had the shallowest point estimates, but corrected comparisons did not establish a consistent morph ordering. The adjusted means provide the clearest description of group differences; detailed slopes and femur–tibia analyses remain exploratory (Tables S15–S16).

## Instar-matched comparisons

Both the within-male per-instar component and the tenth-instar male–female component were supported for all five traits (@tbl-instar-decomposition). The largest Holm-adjusted p-values were `r sprintf("%.3g", max(instar_decomposition$instar_component_holm_p))` and `r sprintf("%.3g", max(instar_decomposition$weapon_component_holm_p))`, respectively. Their coefficients also differed for every trait (largest Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(max(instar_decomposition$component_difference_holm_p))`).

For forelegs, midlegs, eyes and linearised tympanic organ size, the matched male–female component exceeded the per-instar component. Matched male–female differences were `r fmt_num(instar_fore$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_mid$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_eye$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`% and `r fmt_num(instar_ear$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`%, compared with per-instar changes of `r fmt_num(instar_fore$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_mid$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`%, `r fmt_num(instar_eye$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`% and `r fmt_num(instar_ear$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`%. Hindlegs showed the reverse: a `r fmt_num(instar_hind$instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1)`% per-instar change exceeded the `r fmt_num(instar_hind$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1)`% matched male–female difference.

The joint leg decomposition gave similar estimates (per-instar changes `r fmt_num(min(instar_joint_legs$instar_component_pct_per_instar), 1)`–`r fmt_num(max(instar_joint_legs$instar_component_pct_per_instar), 1)`%; matched male–female differences `r fmt_num(min(instar_joint_legs$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female), 1)`–`r fmt_num(max(instar_joint_legs$weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female), 1)`%). The hindleg gradient thus tracked terminal instar number more closely than the same-instar sex contrast. These associations do not establish that extra moults caused the differences, or that the sex contrast measures weapon effects alone.

## Weapon–leg integration

After adjustment for pronotum length, `r hl_n_positive` of `r hl_n_total` head–leg slopes had 95% confidence intervals entirely above zero; no estimated slope was negative (Table S3). The group-by-leg-by-head interaction was supported (`r fmt_f_anova(hl_int_row)`), indicating heterogeneity among partial slopes. Planned morph contrasts were nevertheless `r ifelse(hl_strat_all_ns, "uniformly nonsignificant", "largely nonsignificant")` after Holm adjustment (Table S4), so they did not establish a simple morph ranking in integration strength. Positive weapon–leg association was widespread, but neither identical slopes nor a causal compensation mechanism was demonstrated.

## Sensory morphology

### Adjusted group differences

Group-specific body-size slopes were not supported for ear size (`r fmt_f_nested(ear_body_test)`) or eye length (`r fmt_f_nested(eye_body_test)`), and adjusted comparisons used common-slope models. At 7.2 mm pronotum length, tenth-instar males had tympanic organ areas `r fmt_num(ear_body_strat_tenth_female$area_percent_difference, 1)`% larger than females (Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(ear_body_strat_tenth_female$p.value)`). Eighth-instar males had areas `r fmt_num(abs(ear_body_strat_eighth_tenth$area_percent_difference), 1)`% smaller than tenth-instar males (`r fmt_p(ear_body_strat_eighth_tenth$p.value)`).

Tenth-instar males had eyes `r fmt_num(eye_body_strat_tenth_female$percent_difference, 1)`% longer than females (Holm-adjusted `r fmt_p(eye_body_strat_tenth_female$p.value)`); eighth-instar eyes were `r fmt_num(abs(eye_body_strat_eighth_tenth$percent_difference), 1)`% shorter than tenth-instar eyes (`r fmt_p(eye_body_strat_eighth_tenth$p.value)`). Ninth-instar midpoint contrasts were nonsignificant for both ear (`r fmt_p(ear_body_strat_ninth_mid$p.value)`) and eye (`r fmt_p(eye_body_strat_ninth_mid$p.value)`), with exploratory equivalence tests in Table S13. Sensory dimensions followed the same broad eighth-to-tenth-instar gradient as leg length (@fig-adjusted-traits; Table S17).

### Local associations and weapon–ear covariance

No group difference in partial slope was detected for ear–foretibia (`r fmt_f_nested(ear_local_test)`) or eye–head (`r fmt_f_nested(eye_local_test)`) associations. Confidence intervals were entirely positive for `r ear_local_n_positive` of `r nrow(ear_local_slopes)` ear–foretibia slopes and `r eye_local_n_positive` of `r nrow(eye_local_slopes)` eye–head slopes. These findings describe positive local associations without demonstrating equivalence among groups. Eye–head slopes ranged from `r fmt_num(min(eye_local_slopes[[eye_local_trend_col]]), 2)` to `r fmt_num(max(eye_local_slopes[[eye_local_trend_col]]), 2)` and may partly reflect the shared geometry of the head capsule.

The weapon–ear group-by-head interaction was not supported (`r fmt_f_nested(ear_weapon_test)`). The female slope was positive (`r fmt_num(ear_weapon_female[[ear_weapon_trend_col]], 3)`, 95% confidence interval `r fmt_num(ear_weapon_female$lower.CL, 3)`–`r fmt_num(ear_weapon_female$upper.CL, 3)`; `r fmt_p(ear_weapon_female$p.value)`), whereas none of the three male intervals excluded zero. Male estimates ranged from `r fmt_num(we_male_slope_min, 3)` to `r fmt_num(we_male_slope_max, 3)`, and approximate minimum detectable slopes averaged `r fmt_num(we_mde_mean, 2)` and reached `r fmt_num(we_mde_worst, 2)` (@tbl-weapon-ear-precision). No standardized slope met the illustrative ±0.20 near-zero equivalence criterion (Table S5). Male associations therefore remain imprecise: these results neither demonstrate a negative weapon–ear relationship nor establish negligible association. A significant female slope and nonsignificant male slopes do not themselves establish a sex difference.

## Model diagnostics

Observed and predicted trait distributions corresponded closely. Residuals were approximately normal with broadly homogeneous variance and minor curvature at fitted-range extremes. Diagnostic checks did not identify an observation requiring exclusion after measurement inspection. The log–log models and repeated-trait generalized least-squares specification were retained.

# Discussion

The sampled male morphs showed coordinated divergence in body-size-adjusted locomotor and sensory dimensions. Eighth-instar searching males did not have the longest legs or largest sensory structures; these traits generally increased towards tenth-instar males. This pattern opposed the searching-and-detection prediction. A dominant axis summarized most adjusted group-effect variation, but a smaller departure from rank one was detectable. The findings therefore describe predominantly, rather than exclusively, one-dimensional divergence.

All within-group correlations among the five non-head traits were positive, and no covariance- or correlation-matrix difference was detected for that primary trait set. This is compatible with a shared pattern of integration, not proof of invariant covariance. The six-trait sensitivity detected a covariance-magnitude difference when head size was restored. Because head length contributes to male classification, excluding it addresses an important source of dependence, but the sensitivity result prevents extending the five-trait null result to the entire phenotype.

## Locomotor divergence among strategies

Tenth-instar males had the longest adjusted legs and eighth-instar males the shortest, with ninth-instar estimates close to the midpoint. This intermediate position is consistent with flexible fighting and sneaking [@wilson2019; @kelly2025], but it may also follow from maturation at an intermediate instar. Morphological intermediacy alone does not demonstrate adaptation for behavioural flexibility.

The strongest anterior–posterior allocation contrast involved tenth-instar males and females, rather than two male morphs. Foreleg enlargement could help heavily armed males stabilize the body, maintain purchase or manoeuvre during contests. Comparable support functions have been proposed for weapon-associated leg enlargement in beetles [@tomkins2005; @mccullough2013]. However, these data contain no measurements of leverage, locomotor performance or fighting success, so the proposed function remains untested.

Among male morphs, differences were principally a general leg-length gradient rather than a supported redistribution between anterior and posterior legs. The simple expectation of long-legged searching males contrasted with anteriorly specialized defenders was therefore not supported. Some group variation in body-size scaling was detected, but the three-way interaction and corrected slope comparisons did not resolve a consistent leg-specific morph pattern. Adjusted means provide firmer evidence of morphological divergence than the exploratory slope rankings. Previously reported weapon allometry [@kelly2026] cannot be assumed to apply to supporting structures.

## Positive integration and masked allocation costs

Individuals with relatively larger heads generally had relatively longer legs. This is consistent with secondary sexual trait compensation, in which supporting structures enlarge alongside costly weaponry [@tomkins2005; @husak2011]. It also resembles positive weapon–hindleg integration in exaggerated male European earwigs, *Forficula auricularia* [@tomkins2005]. Both earwigs and tree wētā grow through successive nymphal instars rather than within a closed pupal system, making their developmental comparison relevant. Nevertheless, positive phenotypic associations alone cannot identify compensation or explain differences between hemimetabolous and holometabolous insects.

The acquisition–allocation distinction is central. Variation in acquired resources can generate positive covariance among costly traits even when those traits compete for a limited allocation pool [@vannoordwijk1986]. Resource acquisition was not measured in these field-collected adults. Consequently, the absence of negative covariance means that no negative phenotypic association was detected in the measured primary trait set; it does not rule out underlying developmental costs.

Positive weapon–leg relationships were widespread rather than restricted to the most heavily armed morph. Although the omnibus interaction detected slope heterogeneity, planned contrasts did not establish consistently stronger integration in tenth-instar males. A shared growth process, compensatory development and correlated selection remain possible explanations. The dimensionality and sign results are compatible with shared growth but do not discriminate decisively among those mechanisms. Manipulating acquisition while tracking several traits would provide a more direct test of allocation costs than further cross-sectional correlations alone.

## Sensory divergence and local anatomy

The sensory gradient also ran opposite to the expectation that actively searching eighth-instar males would invest most in detection. This contrasts with relatively larger eyes in small searching *Centris pallida* males [@barrett2021; @barrett2026]. Strategy-associated sensory investment therefore cannot be inferred simply from whether males search or defend. Gallery defence may itself require rival assessment or navigation, or sensory enlargement may accompany a broader developmental programme without being a tactic-specific adaptation.

Male–female differences suggest a separate possibility. All male morphs had relatively longer eyes than females, and ninth- and tenth-instar males had larger tympanic organs. If males are more mobile, a sensory correlate of mate searching might be expressed between sexes rather than among male morphs. Mobility was not measured here, so that interpretation remains a hypothesis. Common-slope sensory models describe shifts in adjusted trait elevation, but common estimated slopes do not establish a shared developmental mechanism. Elevation differences can generate substantial sensory exaggeration without steeper scaling, as reported for crane-fly antennae [@hirani2026].

Neither eye length nor tympanic membrane area measures sensory performance directly. Larger eyes could differ in ommatidial number or sensitivity, or simply reflect head-capsule geometry. Membrane area alone does not specify hearing thresholds or frequency response. These traits are therefore indices of morphological investment whose functional significance requires physiological or behavioural measurements.

Positive ear–foretibia and eye–head associations were expected given their anatomical relationships. Eyes and mandibles occupy the same head capsule, so shared geometry can contribute to eye–head covariance independently of adaptive coordination between vision and weaponry. No local slope differences were detected, but those tests did not establish equivalent associations across groups.

Weapon–ear covariance illustrates why among-group divergence and within-group integration must be separated. Ear area followed the male morph gradient, yet within-male head–ear slopes were imprecise and did not meet the near-zero equivalence criterion. The results support neither developmental independence nor strong male integration. They also do not establish a female–male slope difference. Parallel morph means can coexist with uncertain within-morph associations, and the uncertainty should not be converted into evidence of biological decoupling.

## What the female reference resolves

Females revealed an anterior allocation shift and sensory differences that a male-only comparison would miss. They also supplied the only terminal-instar-matched reference. The per-instar coefficient was larger than the matched sex coefficient for hindlegs, whereas the matched sex coefficient was larger for anterior legs and sensory dimensions. This describes where divergence tracks the male instar gradient and where a larger same-instar sex difference remains.

Females are not an unselected control: their morphology is subject to reproductive, locomotor and sensory demands of its own. Nor does matching terminal instar isolate weapon expression. The comparison still differs in sex, and terminal instar number is not a direct measurement of chronological development time. The two components are useful descriptive contrasts, but cannot assign causal shares of divergence to extra moults and weapons. Longitudinal developmental measurements or manipulations are required for that inference.

## Limitations and future tests

Genetic polymorphism in morph expression makes these comparisons less dependent on nutritionally induced morph determination than many insect polyphenisms [@kelly2024]. It does not remove environmental variation within morphs. Food, temperature, health and developmental history may affect several adult traits together, even at the same final pronotum length. Body-size adjustment cannot eliminate all consequences of different maturation pathways.

Vegetation sampling and unequal group sizes further constrain inference. Gallery occupants may be under-represented, and the sampled morph composition differed from published population references. Unrecorded sampling differences could affect both estimated means and covariance. Tenth-instar males were less numerous than other groups, limiting precision for some slopes and interactions. The reported confidence intervals, equivalence sensitivities and minimum detectable effects make these limitations explicit but do not correct the sampling frame.

Functional experiments could test whether anterior leg dimensions improve stability or contest performance independently of weapon size, and whether eye or tympanic dimensions predict detection under natural conditions. Common-garden studies following genetically assigned morphs through successive instars could separate developmental history from strategy-associated allocation. Combining resource manipulations with estimates of genetic covariance and selection would help distinguish shared growth from adaptive compensation.

## Conclusions

Locomotor and sensory dimensions generally increased from eighth- to tenth-instar males, with most adjusted group divergence concentrated along one dominant axis and smaller detectable departures from it. No negative within-group phenotypic covariance or matrix restructuring was detected in the primary five-trait analysis, but head-inclusive sensitivity results qualify any broader claim of homogeneous covariance. Positive head–leg and local sensory associations do not exclude masked allocation costs, and male weapon–ear integration remains uncertain. Instar-matched female comparisons reveal an additional sex-associated contrast without isolating a causal weapon effect. Alternative mating strategies in this sample are therefore characterized by predominantly coordinated morphological divergence whose developmental and functional causes remain to be tested.

```{r}

instar_display_names <- c(

)

    Trait          = instar_display_names[trait],
    `n`            = n,
    `Per instar (%)` = round(instar_component_pct_per_instar, 1),
    `Per instar P`   = ifelse(instar_component_holm_p < 0.001, "<0.001",
                              sprintf("%.3f", instar_component_holm_p)),
    `Weapon (%)`     = round(weapon_component_pct_male_vs_female, 1),
    `Weapon P`       = ifelse(weapon_component_holm_p < 0.001, "<0.001",
                              sprintf("%.3f", weapon_component_holm_p)),
    `Difference P` = ifelse(component_difference_holm_p < 0.001, "<0.001",
                                      sprintf("%.3f", component_difference_holm_p)),
    `Larger component` = ifelse(component_difference_log < 0,

  manuscript_table(align = c("left", rep("right", 7)))
```

  manuscript_table(align = c("left", "left", "right", "right", "right"))
